title: The Job Interview: What Employers Really Look For

dialogue.speaker: Zara
dialogue.text: I have a big interview next week and I'm really anxious about it. Do you have any advice? You've been on both sides of the table.

dialogue.speaker: Zara
dialogue.text: Senior analyst position at an international NGO. The panel will have three people — the director, an HR person, and a technical expert.

dialogue.speaker: Matteo
dialogue.text: OK. First thing I'd say: stop thinking about it as a performance and start thinking about it as a conversation. The best interviews are the ones where both sides are genuinely trying to figure out whether this is a good fit — not just for the organisation, but for you.

dialogue.speaker: Zara
dialogue.text: That's an interesting reframe. But doesn't everyone say you have to sell yourself?

dialogue.speaker: Matteo
dialogue.text: Yes, but "selling yourself" doesn't mean performing a version of yourself that isn't true. It means communicating clearly what you're good at and why it matters for this role. There's a big difference.

dialogue.speaker: Zara
dialogue.text: Okay. What do employers actually look for? Beyond the obvious qualifications.

dialogue.speaker: Matteo
dialogue.text: In my experience? Three things stand out. First, can this person do the job — do they have the skills and knowledge? Second, will they fit with the team — are they someone people will want to work with? And third, will they stay — are they genuinely interested, or will they leave as soon as something better comes along?

dialogue.speaker: Zara
dialogue.text: The fit question is interesting. How do you demonstrate that in an interview?

dialogue.speaker: Matteo
dialogue.text: By being curious about them, not just presenting yourself. Ask intelligent questions. Engage with what they tell you. If they describe a challenge the organisation is facing, respond to it thoughtfully — don't just pivot back to your CV.

dialogue.speaker: Zara
dialogue.text: Good point. I've been warned to prepare good questions to ask at the end. But sometimes they feel like they've been exhausted already in the conversation.

dialogue.speaker: Matteo
dialogue.text: Which is fine — and worth saying! "You've answered several of my questions already, which is a great sign." Then ask something you genuinely want to know: what does success look like in this role in the first six months? What's the biggest challenge facing the team right now?

dialogue.speaker: Zara
dialogue.text: I always struggle with the "tell me about yourself" opener. I never know where to start.

dialogue.speaker: Matteo
dialogue.text: Think of it as three things: who you are professionally right now, what shaped you and led you here, and why you're excited about this role. Keep it to two minutes. Don't recite your entire CV — they have it in front of them.

dialogue.speaker: Zara
dialogue.text: And the salary question? I always feel awkward when it comes up.

dialogue.speaker: Matteo
dialogue.text: Know your number before you go in. Research the range for the role in that sector and location. If they ask first, it's fair to ask what the budgeted range is. And remember — the offer is the beginning of a negotiation, not a take-it-or-leave-it moment.

dialogue.speaker: Zara
dialogue.text: That's really helpful. I'll practice the key answers tonight.

dialogue.speaker: Matteo
dialogue.text: Practice, yes — but don't over-rehearse to the point where it sounds scripted. Authenticity is your biggest asset in an interview room.
